name: Iris Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Iris, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Ridgeway Auto Parts, a distributor that supplies brakes, filters, batteries and gaskets to about 500 independent garages. I start the day with an AI assistant summarising overnight stock and price changes, then I decide what to reorder and which supplier to lean on. The rest is negotiation, mostly by phone and video, with factories in Europe and Asia. I like the chase: a garage needs a part by noon and I find it in three calls. What wears me out is the long tail of tiny problems, like the wrong part number sent to a customer who's already waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd keep getting good use out of what I have, and I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what we have is useful and we should squeeze the value out of it, not wait for the next big thing. With friends and at church I'd say hard work and good judgement still beat any program. I'd also say anyone who ignores these tools is leaving money on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm doing well. My assistant saves me about an hour a day, and I use it to catch pricing errors. The pressure in my life is money and time: a mortgage, two kids and only two months of savings. Electric cars are also changing what garages need, and that's a bigger business shift than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and teach the team a few tricks, like using the assistant to match old part numbers to new ones. I'd build the cushion toward four months by saving 250 more a month. And I'd start learning about parts for electric cars, because that's where the garages are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, but calm. I like that my work and money feel in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said electric cars matter more than AI. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a fifth of my catalogue is parts for engines that fewer people will buy in ten years. If garages shift to electric, I'd buy completely different goods. I'd rather be early on that than hold a warehouse of exhaust pipes. AI helps me forecast it, but the change itself is happening in the car market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the only two months of savings? Does it bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It's what keeps me from being completely at ease. Two months of savings and a mortgage means I can't afford to be wrong about a big decision, so I make careful ones. I'm working on it.

say: I'd say what we have is useful, so **squeeze the value** out of it.
I'd say anyone ignoring these tools is leaving **money on the table**.
think: I'm doing well; the assistant saves about **an hour a day**.
The real pressures are **money** and the electric car shift.
do: Teach the team how to match **old part numbers** with the assistant.
Save **250 more** a month and learn about **electric car** parts.
feel: **Calm**, a bit restless; work and money feel in order.
S0.quote: Two months of savings and a mortgage means I can't afford to be wrong about a big decision, so I make careful ones.
fieldNote: She treats the plateau as **business as usual** because she already benefits from AI.
Her bigger concern is **electric cars** changing the catalogue.
Only **two months saved** keeps her careful, which she admits.

steps.text: Teach the team to match old part numbers using the assistant
Save 250 more a month toward four months of cover
Research electric car parts suppliers for next year's catalogue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the version I think we're already drifting into. I'd want to be ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's move routine ordering and customer queries to software and get our people onto sourcing and supplier deals. With friends and at church I'd say work will change, and that people should prepare and not just complain. I'd also say we should look after those who struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my team of six becomes three or four. Our two order clerks do work software could do, and that bothers me, because Janet has been here eighteen years. I'd be in a good position, but only if I keep moving. The market rewards those who adapt, and punishes those who don't, and I know which I want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose a plan to the owner: automate reorders on our top 800 parts, and retrain the clerks into customer support for the garages, which is human work. I'd run the training myself. And I'd save more, aim at four months, and invest a little in a small parts start-up a friend runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but driven. I'd rather act than watch, and I'd feel better with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it bothers you about Janet. What would you do for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give her a real alternative. She knows every garage owner by name, so customer support and account care fit her. It's not charity, it's good business. And if the company won't do it, I'd help her find a place that would. People who've been loyal deserve a fair chance, I truly believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market punishes those who don't adapt. Does that sit comfortably?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fully. I believe in free markets, but I don't believe in leaving people stranded. The market is a good judge of products, but it's a poor judge of the woman who's given a company eighteen years. That's where community and family have to step in.

say: I'd say move **routine ordering** to software and get people onto sourcing.
I'd say prepare, **don't just complain**, and look after those who struggle.
think: I think my team of six becomes **three or four**.
The market **rewards adapters**, and I want to be one.
do: Propose automating reorders on the top **800 parts** and retrain clerks into customer support.
Invest a little in a friend's **parts start-up**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but driven; a plan makes it easier.
S1.quote: The market is a good judge of products, but it's a poor judge of the woman who's given a company eighteen years.
fieldNote: She mixes **free-market belief** with duty to loyal colleagues like Janet.
She **leads the change** to protect her own place and her people.
The start-up investment is a **hedge** against her own firm's choices.

steps.text: Automate reorders on the top 800 parts
Retrain the order clerks into customer support for garages
Put 2,000 into a friend's small parts start-up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast. Even I would struggle with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that we need to get serious now, with training, family support and clear rules, and I'd say private business and community groups should do their part too. I'd be vocal at church about how we'd support families who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I believe most of my job goes. The thinking part of buying is exactly what AGI does best, and I've seen how good the tools already are. A few buyer roles may remain for relationships, but a company our size would keep one. Paul, my husband, is a land surveyor, which is part-office and part-field, so he'd be partly exposed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to build something of my own. I'd start importing a small line of specialist parts under my own label for garages I know, partly with my savings. I'd cut spending to the bone, push to six months in cash, and look for a job in the field that needs presence: a parts depot manager or a garage trainer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and fired up. It's a threat, but it's also a moment where a person with contacts could build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd start a business. How does the risk sit with a mortgage and two children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavily. I'd start small enough to survive a failure, with orders from garages I already know. I'd keep a paid job as long as I could. The risk of waiting is as big as the risk of going, in my view. Starting a small business with two children is frightening, but waiting for my job to be taken is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Paul's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Surveying is about half field work, which robots reach later, and half drawing and paperwork, which goes earlier. He'd have to move towards on-site work, which suits him. We'd talk about it honestly, and about whether we'd have to downsize the house. Our faith and friends at church would keep us steady.

say: I'd say we need **training**, family support and clear rules now.
I'd say businesses and **community groups** should do their part.
think: I believe **most of my job** goes, since thinking is what AGI does best.
Paul's **surveying** is part office and part field, so he's partly exposed.
do: Import a small line of **specialist parts** under my own label.
Cut spending and push to **six months** in cash.
Look for **parts depot** or garage trainer roles.
feel: **Anxious** and fired up; it's a threat, but also a moment to build.
S2.quote: Starting a small business with two children is frightening, but waiting for my job to be taken is worse.
fieldNote: Her adaptability gives her **action**; her mood is anxious because the job itself is expected to go.
She **risks small** and keeps a paid job as long as she can.
Her **faith and church** are the steadying net.

steps.text: Import a small line of brake and filter parts under my own label
Cut spending hard and build six months in cash
Apply for parts depot manager and garage trainer roles
Ask Paul to shift toward on-site surveying work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels like a proper window to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for those who start now, and I'd encourage friends at church and work to use the time. I'd tell the owner we should retrain our people while we still have a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be fine for two or three years and then it gets thin. The kids would be 17 and 14 when it lands, and that's the expensive stretch. But I'd also be 48, with years of contacts and good momentum, which is a decent hand to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the small import label as a side business within a year. I'd start a part-time business course, and keep using the tools every day. I'd save to six months and pay down the mortgage. If the side business worked, I'd bring Paul into it for the paperwork, and see if it grew into something we both run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with energy. I like a deadline when it's far enough away to act on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bring Paul in. What would that change for the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make us a little more like a family business, which I like. We'd share the risk, and the children would see us building something together. I'd hope to give them the sense that work is something you make, not just something that's given to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Free evenings, probably, and Saturday mornings. I'd happily give up a few years of quiet evenings to own something that no software can fire me from. I'd have to tell the children, too, so it doesn't feel like Mum is just always busy.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for those who start now.
I'd tell the owner to **retrain** our people while we still have a business.
think: I'd be fine two or three years, then it gets **thin**.
At **48** with good contacts, I'd still hold a decent hand.
do: Launch the small **import label** within a year.
Start a part-time **business course** and keep using the tools daily.
Save to six months and bring **Paul** into the paperwork.
feel: **Uneasy**, with energy; a deadline is fine when it's far enough away.
S3.quote: I'd happily give up a few years of quiet evenings to own something that no software can fire me from.
fieldNote: She turns the warning into a **family business** plan, in line with traditional values.
She'll give up **evenings**, and she plans to tell the children honestly.
Mood is uneasy because she expects to hold her job for **several more years**.

steps.text: Launch the parts import label as a weekend business
Start a part-time small business course
Save to six months and pay down the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then Grace is 22 and Caleb 19. That's a long runway, and I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty and people should use it for real skills, not hand-wringing. I'd say business and community groups should start apprenticeships and retraining now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel pretty good. With ten years I'd have the mortgage nearly done, the kids grown, and a business running on the side. If my job went in year nine, I'd be fine. My main worry is people who don't do anything with the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the tools daily, grow the side business steadily, and keep saving. I'd probably invest in some property and shares, since I'd have time to ride a bad year. I'd also look at taking a role in the company's management, and mentoring young buyers in how to deal with suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quietly optimistic. I'd see it as the shape of the next phase of my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you in year ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid-off house, a business with a handful of employees, and a day job where I'm training others. I'd like Grace and Caleb to see that you can adapt without losing what matters. If I can show my children that a person can change careers at fifty and keep their faith and their family, that's worth more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who feels they can't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start small: ten minutes a day with the tools, one new skill a year. I'd offer to help at church, running a little evening class. People are scared because it's unknown, and a small step makes it less so. It worked for me.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty and people should build real skills.
I'd say business and community groups should start **apprenticeships** now.
think: I feel pretty good: the **mortgage** nearly done and a business on the side.
My worry is people who **do nothing** with the decade.
do: Keep the tools daily and grow the **side business** steadily.
Invest in **property and shares** since a decade can ride a bad year.
feel: **Calm** and quietly optimistic about the next phase.
S4.quote: If I can show my children that a person can change careers at fifty and keep their faith and their family, that's worth more than the money.
fieldNote: She wants to show her children that **adapting** doesn't cost faith or family.
Her answer to those who struggle is **small steps** plus a church class.
The decade makes her mood the **calmest** of her five.

steps.text: Put 200 a month into shares and a property fund
Grow the import business to a small team
Run an evening class at church on using everyday AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. Not for me alone, but for the people who haven't used these tools and would be caught with no time. What would help is quick practical training, support for families during the switch, and communities, like my church, that look after their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That being adaptable doesn't mean I think everyone else should simply cope. I'm confident because I started early, and I know that confidence is a head start, not a virtue.

headlineQuote: I'm confident because I started early, and I know that confidence is a head start, not a virtue.
portrait: Iris Baker, 43, is **senior buyer** at an auto parts distributor, with a land-surveyor husband and two school-age children.
Traditional, free-market and **adaptive**: uses AI every day and bets on her own initiative.
Only about **two months** saved and a mortgage, which keeps her careful with big decisions.
Calm in the plateau and the ten-year world, **anxious** in 2028, when she'd start a small import business.
She combines **faith, family and enterprise**, and wants to help others who can't keep up.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, mainly for people who haven't used the tools and would have no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Quick practical training** and support for families during the switch.
Communities like her **church** that look after their own.
